Q: How to run jq from gitbash in Windows? A:

In my case, I have fixed it in Windows10 while practicing a scenario of "Techworld with Nana" course, as per the below steps:

  1. open "cmd" prompt (Run as administrator)

  2. curl -L -o /usr/bin/jq-win64.exe

    Download it here

  3. You can add C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin path to your environment variables. If you follow this step, ignore the below steps.

    [OR]

    Go to the directory where jq is downloaded: C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin and copy the file to C:\ drive

  4. Add the path C:\ to "path" environment variable. This PC → Properties → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables → Edit → New. Then add the path (where you copied jq.exe, i.e., C:\) and Save it.

  5. Now open a new "cmd" prompt, jq --version

Q: Purpose of the crossorigin attribute...? A:

The crossorigin attribute in HTML elements like <img>, <script>, <audio>, and <video> is used to configure the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) settings when fetching resources from a different origin.

Why is it needed?

By default, browsers send cross-origin requests for media or scripts without requesting CORS authorization. While the resource will still load, its usage within the browser becomes restricted due to security mechanisms (e.g., Same-Origin Policy):

  • For <script> tags: Errors occurring inside a cross-origin script will be masked as a generic "Script error." on window.onerror unless CORS is explicitly enabled using crossorigin.
  • For <img> tags: Loading a cross-origin image onto a Canvas element without crossorigin will mark the canvas as "tainted," preventing operations like toDataURL() or getImageData().

Attribute Values

The crossorigin attribute supports two primary keyword values:

  1. anonymous (or just crossorigin=""):

    • Sends a CORS request with an Origin header.
    • Does not include credentials (such as cookies, HTTP authentication, or TLS client certificates) in the request.
    • If the server responds with an appropriate Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, the resource can be safely accessed without browser restrictions.

  2. use-credentials:

    • Sends a CORS request that includes user credentials (cookies, authentication headers).
    • The server must explicitly respond with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true along with matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers for the request to succeed.

For a complete breakdown with detailed examples and edge cases, feel free to check out my detailed guide: HTML crossorigin Attribute – Specifying CORS Request Modes.

(Full disclosure: I am the author of the linked article.)
